growth_story.headline: Lithuania's income per person collapsed in the early 1990s, boomed after 2000, crashed in 2009 and has since grown more slowly to a new peak in 2025.
growth_story.arc: After independence, trade with the former Soviet republics broke down and energy import prices jumped, and income per person shrank by 2.8 percent a year over 1991–1999, with the worst fall in 1992 (-21.2). From 2000 to 2007 it grew 8.7 percent a year, a boom during which, the IMF says, large imbalances built up after Lithuania joined the EU in 2004. The boom ended abruptly: income per person fell 13.9 percent in 2009, and a painful fall in costs and prices, which the IMF calls an internal devaluation, set up an export-led recovery. Since 2008 growth has averaged 3.0 percent a year, with 3.3 over 2016–2025 against 4.2 in the decade before, and the IMF credits productivity growth for fast catch-up with the euro area until Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Income per person slipped in 2023 (-0.7), grew 2.4 percent in 2024 and 2.9 percent in 2025, and reached its highest level yet in 2025.

threads.title: Soviet trade collapse
threads.text: At independence, Lithuania lost its old markets in the former Soviet Union and had to pay far more for Russian oil and gas. The World Bank tied the early output fall mainly to these trade disruptions, and income per person fell every year from 1991 to 1994.

threads.title: EU accession boom and bust
threads.text: After EU entry in 2004, the IMF says large imbalances built up: the real exchange rate rose, competitiveness slipped and the current account deficit widened. When the boom ended, wages and prices fell instead, and the IMF says this painful adjustment laid the base for an export-led recovery.

threads.title: Productivity-led catch-up
threads.text: From the 2009 crash until 2022, the IMF says Lithuania caught up fast with the euro area, mainly through rising productivity and a strong export performance, especially in services. The export-led recovery held up even after trade sanctions on Russia in 2015 cost it export market share.

threads.text: Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 brought an energy shock, and income per person grew only 1.6 percent in 2022 and fell in 2023. Defense spending is now rising sharply, and the IMF counts it, with ageing, among the long-term pressures on public spending.

growth_story.tension: The IMF writes of a remarkable performance since the 2008 crisis and rapid catch-up with the euro area. The data tell a rougher story: the era since 2008 averages 3.0 percent a year against 8.7 in 2000–2007, it opens with a 13.9 percent fall in 2009, and the tool classes Lithuania's growth as volatile. The IMF also describes a shrinking and ageing society, so part of the rise in income per person comes from fewer people rather than more output.
